title: Dhurandhar 2 Lands on Netflix India Today. The Most-Watched Indian Film in History Just Got Another Stage.
excerpt: Ranveer Singh's 1,800-crore revenge epic crossed 70 million digital views, lapped RRR, and is now streaming on Netflix India — while the diaspora has had the uncut 'Raw & Undekha' version for over a month.
body:
Some films refuse to stop winning. **Dhurandhar 2: The Revenge** has already conquered the box office, rewritten the streaming record books, and become the most-watched Indian film in digital history — and as of today, June 19, it has one more crown to claim. **Ranveer Singh's** blood-soaked action epic has landed on **Netflix India**, throwing open the gates to an audience that had been waiting on the other side of a paywall.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=NHk7scrb_9I</youtube>

https://x.com/NetflixIndia/status/2067973211095220721

The numbers behind this film read like a typo. After a theatrical run that grossed more than 1,800 crore worldwide — placing it among the highest-grossing Indian films ever made — the **Aditya Dhar**-directed spectacle premiered on JioHotstar on June 5 and immediately detonated. It pulled a staggering 50 million viewers in its opening weekend alone, the biggest digital debut any Indian film has ever recorded, and has since crossed 70 million views. That figure doesn't just beat the field; it laps *RRR*, the previous benchmark, which managed a little over 50 million.

> The most-watched Indian film digitally across all platforms — a record that didn't exist in this shape until Dhurandhar walked in and rewrote it.

Now comes the Netflix India chapter. The film's journey across platforms has been almost as dramatic as its plot. The uncut version — marketed as the *Raw & Undekha* cut, complete with unmuted profanity, extended gore, and sequences trimmed for the theatrical A-certificate — first hit Netflix internationally on May 15. JioHotstar held the India streaming rights, premiering the uncut version domestically on June 5 after a starry grand digital premiere on June 4. And now, on June 19, Netflix India joins the party, widening the film's reach to yet another swath of subscribers at home.

For the **diaspora**, this is the headline. Dhurandhar 2 has been available on Netflix in international territories since mid-May, meaning NRIs in the US, UK, Canada, and beyond have had access to the *Raw & Undekha* cut for over a month — the full, unflinching, 235-minute experience, exactly as the overseas theatrical screenings ran it. If you've been putting it off, the algorithm is about to make it very hard to ignore, because the film is now simultaneously dominating Netflix libraries on both sides of the ocean.

A word on that cut, because it matters. **Aditya Dhar** built Dhurandhar as a brutal, maximalist revenge saga, and the streaming version doesn't sand down its edges — it sharpens them. The CBFC's theatrical edit shaved violent scenes and profanities down to a 229-minute runtime in India; the digital *Raw & Undekha* cut puts much of it back. This is not the polished-for-TV version. It's the one Dhar wanted you to see, and it's a large part of why the OTT numbers exploded the way they did. Audiences didn't just rewatch a hit — they came for footage they couldn't get in the theatre.

**Ranveer Singh**, for his part, has rarely been more commanding. Coming off a stretch where critics wondered whether he'd find a role big enough for his outsized screen energy, Dhurandhar handed him exactly that — a character built on rage, restraint, and spectacle in equal measure. His father-in-law **Prakash Padukone** offered a wry, honest verdict that there was "a little too much violence" for his taste, which is perhaps the most on-brand thing a legendary badminton champion could say about his son-in-law's 1,800-crore bloodbath. The audience, evidently, disagreed with the squeamishness.

The trailer alone had foreshadowed all of this, racking up a barely-believable 312 million views across platforms before release and turning the March 19 theatrical launch — timed to Gudi Padwa, Ugadi, and Eid — into a genuine event. Banned across the Gulf Cooperation Council countries, like its predecessor, the film became something close to forbidden fruit in certain markets, which only fed the global curiosity.

So what does a Netflix India drop add to a film that has already won everything? Reach, and longevity. Streaming records are a snapshot; a permanent berth on the world's biggest platform is a long tail. Dhurandhar 2 is now positioned to keep finding new viewers for months, in living rooms from Mumbai to New Jersey. The revenge, it turns out, is far from over — it's just moving to a screen near you.
